core_obligations: The multisection identities at proof lines 311-313: the generating function of each statistic in a residue class is written as a finite average of the corresponding root-of-unity evaluations, which is the step that turns the problem into one about J at roots of unity.

The plan of the argument at proof line 316: Wright's circle method is applied to show that the j = 0 term dominates the asymptotics for each statistic, which is what makes the main term independent of the residue class and hence gives equidistribution.

The discussion of the other poles at proof line 318: the author invokes the published domination result for the pole at q = 1 and explains, case by case, which assumption on s prevents another pole from contributing at the same order.

The major-arc evaluation at proof lines 321-327: the bound on the Lerch transcendent, together with the asymptotics of F_{a,c} at 1, gives the three explicit main terms for H_E, H_T and H_G, and Euler's reflection formula reduces the constant in the first of them to the displayed form.

The minor-arc estimate at proof lines 330-340: the proof estimates F_{a,c} on the minor arcs, reduces the products to the F_{a,c} factors and concludes that the major arc dominates exponentially, which yields the claimed equidistribution.
proof_roadmap: Write the generating function of each statistic restricted to a residue class as a multisection, i.e. a finite average of root-of-unity evaluations.
Combine the asymptotics of F_{a,c} and of the reciprocal q-Pochhammer product into asymptotics of the three J at a primitive root of unity.
Evaluate the j = 0 term of the multisection on the major arc with those asymptotics, using the special case zeta = 1 for each statistic.
Check that no other pole contributes at the same order under the stated assumptions on s.
Bound the remaining terms on the minor arcs to conclude that the major arc dominates, so the main term is independent of the residue class.
